10200.doc:
`wlog h : P` adds an assumption `h : P` to the main goal, and adds a side goal that
requires showing that the case `h : ¬ P` can be reduced to the case where `P` holds
(typically by symmetry). The side goal will be at the top of the stack. In this side goal,
there will be two additional assumptions:
- `h : ¬ P`: the assumption that `P` does not hold
- `this`: which is the statement that in the old context `P` suffices to prove the goal.
  By default, the entire context is reverted to produce `this`.

* `wlog h : P with H` gives the name `H` to the statement that `P` proves the goal.
* `wlog h : P generalizing x y ...` reverts certain parts of the context before creating the new
  goal. In this way, the wlog-claim `this` can be applied to `x` and `y` in different orders
  (exploiting symmetry, which is the typical use case).
* `wlog! h : P` also calls `push Not` at the generated hypothesis `h`.
  `wlog! h : P ∧ Q` will transform `¬ (P ∧ Q)` to `P → ¬ Q`
* `wlog! +distrib h : P` also calls `push +distrib Not` at the generated hypothesis `h`.
  `wlog! +distrib h : P ∧ Q` will transform `¬ (P ∧ Q)` to `¬P ∨ ¬Q`.

`η_{+,H}(t) = h_H(t) · t · e^{−t²/2}`. Here `h_H` is the repository's
`TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.hH H`, `h_H(t) = ∫_{y>0} h(t/y) F_H(y) dy/y`. It uses `h = hBase` of (7.5)
and `F_H(y) = sin(H log y)/(π log y)` of (7.6), as in [H]. (7.6) writes `F_H(t)` and
`(h *_M F_H)(y)`, typos for `F_H(y)` and `(h *_M F_H)(t)`; we read `h_H` as a function of `t`. At
`y = 1`, Lean's `F_H` takes the value `0/0 = 0`; this single point does not change the integral.

1060.doc:
**[H, Proposition 9.4.2]**, as printed (p. 187, (9.69)–(9.70)).

How the statement is transcribed:
* "Let `η = η₊` be as in (9.63) for some `H ≥ 25`" becomes `∀ H : ℝ, 25 ≤ H → …`, with `η₊` the
  book's `η_{+,H} = Prop_9_4_2.etaPlusH H`. The proposition is claimed for each such `H`. The
  repository's `etaPlus` fixes `H = 200`, so it cannot be reused directly. `etaPlusH` reuses the
  repository's `hH`, which agrees with (7.5)–(7.6).
* "`x ≥ 10³`, `δ ∈ ℝ`" becomes `∀ x : ℝ, 1e3 ≤ x → ∀ δ : ℝ, …`.
* "`χ` a primitive character mod `q`, `q ≥ 1`" becomes
  `∀ (q : ℕ) [NeZero q] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ q), χ.IsPrimitive → …`. For `q : ℕ`,
  `NeZero q` means `q ≥ 1`. Mathlib's `IsPrimitive` means that the conductor equals `q`.
* "all non-trivial zeros `ρ` of `L(s, χ)` with `|Im ρ| ≤ T₀` lie on the critical line" becomes the
  repository's `TernaryGoldbach.MajorArcs.GRHUpTo χ T₀`. This says that every zero of Mathlib's
  `χ.LFunction` with `0 < Re ρ < 1` and `|Im ρ| ≤ T₀` has `Re ρ = 1/2`. For primitive `χ` these are
  exactly the non-trivial zeros: there are no zeros on `Re s = 1`, and on `Re s = 0` only the
  trivial zero `s = 0` of an even `χ ≠ 1`. For `q = 1`, `χ.LFunction = ζ`.
* "where `T₀ ≥ H + max(10π|δ|, 50)`" becomes `∀ T₀ : ℝ, H + max (10 * π * |δ|) 50 ≤ T₀ → …`. `T₀`
  is quantified universally, since the error term depends on it.
* `Σ_{n=1}^∞ Λ(n) χ(n) e(δn/x) η₊(n/x)` becomes the repository's
  `Schar χ (fun n => Λ n * η(n/x)) (δ/x) = Σ' n, Λ(n) η(n/x) χ(n) e(n · δ/x)`. The `n = 0` term
  vanishes since `Λ 0 = 0`. The series converges absolutely (see
  `Prop_9_4_2.norm_Schar_etaPlusH_le`), so the `tsum` is the series.
* `η̂₊(−δ)` becomes Mathlib's Fourier transform `𝓕 (fun u => (η u : ℂ)) (−δ)`, which is
  `∫ e^{−2πiuw} f(u) du`. This is [H]'s normalization `f̂(t) = ∫ e(−xt) f(x) dx` of §2.1, applied
  to `η₊` extended by `0` to `t < 0` (`Prop_9_4_2.etaPlusH_of_nonpos`).
* The two cases `q = 1` and `q > 1` become the main term `if q = 1 then η̂₊(−δ) · x else 0`.
* `O*(err) · x` becomes `‖Σ − main‖ ≤ err · x`, which is the same thing since `x > 0`
  (`Prop_9_4_2.ostar_iff`).
* `err_{η₊,χ}(δ, x)` is `Prop_9_4_2.errBook H q T₀ δ x`, (9.70) verbatim. The constants are copied
  as printed. `log` is the natural logarithm, `log qT₀ = log(q T₀)` and `log(qT₀/2π) = log(q T₀/(2π))`.
  `√` is `Real.sqrt`, and `x^{1/2}`, `x^{−1}`, `x^{−3/2}` are real powers. At `δ = 0`, [H]'s
  `16.147 |δ| e^{−0.1065 (T₀'/(πδ))²}` is a `0 · e^{−∞}` limit with value `0`. Lean's
  `T₀'/(π · 0) = 0` gives `16.147 · 0 · e⁰ = 0`, the same value. The stray commas at the ends of the
  lines of (9.70) are ignored.
* The second line of (9.70) keeps the printed `x^{1/2}` (see the module docstring). The intended
  `x^{−1/2}` is `prop_9_4_2_corrected`.

`nth_rw` is a variant of `rw` that only changes the `n₁, ..., nₖ`ᵗʰ _occurrence_ of the expression
to be rewritten. Like `rw`, and unlike `nth_rewrite`, it will try to close the goal by trying `rfl`
afterwards. `nth_rw n₁ ... nₖ [eq₁, eq₂,..., eqₘ]` will rewrite the `n₁, ..., nₖ`ᵗʰ _occurrence_ of
each of the `m` equalities `eqᵢ`in that order. Occurrences are counted beginning with `1` in
order of precedence. For example,
```lean
example (h : a = 1) : a + a + a + a + a = 5 := by
  nth_rw 2 3 [h]
/-
a: ℕ
h: a = 1
⊢ a + 1 + 1 + a + a = 5
-/
```
Notice that the second and third occurrences of `a` from the left have been rewritten by
`nth_rw`.

To understand the importance of order of precedence, consider the example below
```lean
example (a b c : Nat) : (a + b) + c = (b + a) + c := by
  nth_rewrite 2 [Nat.add_comm] -- ⊢ (b + a) + c = (b + a) + c
```
Here, although the occurrence parameter is `2`, `(a + b)` is rewritten to `(b + a)`. This happens
because in order of precedence, the first occurrence of `_ + _` is the one that adds `a + b` to `c`.
The occurrence in `a + b` counts as the second occurrence.

If a term `t` is introduced by rewriting with `eqᵢ`, then this instance of `t` will be counted as an
_occurrence_ of `t` for all subsequent rewrites of `t` with `eqⱼ` for `j > i`. This behaviour is
illustrated by the example below
```lean
example (h : a = a + b) : a + a + a + a + a = 0 := by
  nth_rw 3 [h, h]
/-
a b: ℕ
h: a = a + b
⊢ a + a + (a + b + b) + a + a = 0
-/
```
Here, the first `nth_rw` with `h` introduces an additional occurrence of `a` in the goal. That is,
the goal state after the first rewrite looks like below
```lean
/-
a b: ℕ
h: a = a + b
⊢ a + a + (a + b) + a + a = 0
-/
```
This new instance of `a` also turns out to be the third _occurrence_ of `a`.  Therefore,
the next `nth_rw` with `h` rewrites this `a`.

Further, `nth_rw` will close the remaining goal with `rfl` if possible.

with `∏_{3 ≤ p ≤ r₀} p/(p − 1) ≤ 15.5` (`MajorArcs.prod_p_div_le`, from the kernel computation of

12612.doc:
**Minor arcs** [H, (14.49)]:
`∫_{(ℝ/ℤ) \ 𝔐_{8,r₀}} |S_{η_*}(α,x)| |S_{η₊}(α,x)|² dα ≤ 1.0376 x²/κ` for `x ≥ 4.9 · 10²⁶`
(true for `x = xOf N` when `N ≥ 10²⁷`, [H, (14.15)]).

*Proved* (`MinorArcs/MinorTotal.lean: minor_total`) by "repair 3" of [H, Thm 13.2.1] (NOTES, "Ch. 13:
scale erratum"): [H]'s proof derives its ℓ∞ input only off the arcs at scale `x/κ`; we run
Prop 13.1.2 with the arcs at scale `x/κ` above the base level, take a fresh Dirichlet
approximation at each scale in (11.9), extend the levels to `≈ x^{0.3}`, and bound the base gap
with [H, Cor 7.1.3]. It uses Theorem 3.1.1, Prop 12.2.4 (with `c₊ = 2`), the Part II results
`cor_7_1_3`, `prop_7_1_5`, `l2_major_14_7` (`MinorArcs/PartIICited.lean`) and `E_le_14_28`
(`MinorArcs/EBound.lean`), all proved. The numerics (`numerics_M`) are proved: generated cells for
`x ≤ 4.9·10¹⁰¹` (`scripts/gen_cells.py`) and an analytic argument beyond.

(Our constant `1.0376` is weaker than [H]'s `1.00948`. [H]'s Theorem 3.1.1 has `0.5` where its
proof gives `0.8102`; with the corrected [H, (5.36)] our Theorem 3.1.1 has `0.8764`.)

13841.doc:
**The circle method criterion.**  Let `a, b, c` be weights supported on primes `≤ X`.
Split `(0, 1]` into major arcs `𝔐` and minor arcs `𝔪 = (0,1] \ 𝔐`.  If the major arc
contribution has real part `≥ L`, `|S_a| ≤ B` on the minor arcs, and
`B ‖b‖₂ ‖c‖₂ < L`, then `N` is a sum of three primes.

This is exactly the shape of Helfgott's argument: the paper's major-arc theorem gives `L`,
its minor-arc theorem gives `B`, and the remaining work is checking the final inequality.

13848.doc:
The `let` tactic is for adding definitions to the local context of the main goal.
The definition can be unfolded, unlike definitions introduced by `have`.

* `let x : t := e` adds the definition `x : t := e` if `e` is a term of type `t`.
* `let x := e` uses the type of `e` for `t`.
* `let : t := e` and `let := e` use `this` for the name of the hypothesis.
* `let pat := e` for a pattern `pat` is equivalent to `match e with | pat => _`,
  where `_` stands for the tactics that follow this one.
  It is convenient for types that let only one applicable constructor.
  For example, given `p : α × β × γ`, `let ⟨x, y, z⟩ := p` produces the
  local variables `x : α`, `y : β`, and `z : γ`.
* The syntax `let (eq := h) pat := e` is equivalent to `match h : e with | pat => _`,
  which adds the equation `h : e = pat` to the local context.

The tactic supports all the same syntax variants and options as the `let` term.

## Properties and relations

* Unlike `have`, it is possible to unfold definitions introduced using `let`, using tactics
  such as `simp`, `dsimp`, `unfold`, and `subst`.
* The `clear_value` tactic turns a `let` definition into a `have` definition after the fact.
  The tactic might fail if the local context depends on the value of the variable.
* The `let` tactic is preferred for data (non-propositions).
* Sometimes `have` is used for non-propositions to ensure that the variable is never unfolded,
  which may be important for performance reasons.

13849.doc:
`replace h := e` is like `have h := e`, but it removes a previous hypothesis
of the same name as this one if possible. For example, if the state is:

```lean
f : α → β
h : α
⊢ goal
```

Then after `replace h := f h` the state will be:

```lean
f : α → β
h : β
⊢ goal
```

whereas `have h := f h` would result in:

```lean
f : α → β
h† : α
h : β
⊢ goal
```

The tactic `specialize h a₁ ... aₙ` is a way to write `replace h := h a₁ ... aₙ`,
automatically inferring which hypothesis should be replaced.

The `replace` tactic can be used to simulate Rocq's `apply at` tactic.

typeclass can be used for "seminormed spaces" too, just as `Module` can be used for

1484.doc:
**[H, Proposition 9.3.2]**, as printed (p. 182).

How the statement is transcribed:
* The weight `η(t) = t² e^{−t²/2}` is `TernaryGoldbach.MajorArcs.phiPos`: `t² e^{−t²/2}` for
  `t > 0` and `0` for `t ≤ 0`. In [H], `η` is a function on `ℝ₀⁺` (Lemma 9.1.1). Its Fourier
  transform is that of the extension by zero: the proof of Lemma 9.1.1 identifies the main term
  `G_δ(1) = ∫₀^∞ η(t) e(δt) dt` with `η̂(−δ)`. Both functions vanish at `t = 0`, so `phiPos` is
  exactly this extension. In the sum, only the values at `n/x > 0` matter.
* "`x ≥ 1`, `δ ∈ ℝ`" becomes `∀ x : ℝ, 1 ≤ x → ∀ δ : ℝ`.
* "`χ` a primitive character mod `q`, `q ≥ 1`" becomes `q : ℕ` with `[NeZero q]`,
  `χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ q` and `χ.IsPrimitive`, which says the conductor is `q`. Mathlib's
  `χ n` vanishes when `gcd(n, q) > 1`, as in [H]. For `q = 1` the only character is the trivial
  one, and `L(s, χ) = ζ(s)`.
* The hypothesis on zeros becomes `GRHUpTo χ T0`, the repository's definition: every zero `ρ` of
  `χ.LFunction` with `0 < ℜρ < 1` and `|ℑρ| ≤ T₀` has `ℜρ = 1/2`. [H]'s "non-trivial zeros" are
  those in the critical strip. Classically, `L(s, χ)` has no zeros on `ℜs = 1`, and none on
  `ℜs = 0` except the trivial zero at `s = 0` for even `χ ≠ 1`. So this is the same hypothesis.
  `T₀` is any real number that satisfies the next hypothesis.
* "`T₀ ≥ max(10π|δ|, 50)`" becomes `max (10 * π * |δ|) 50 ≤ T0`, as in the Lean theorem.
* `Σ_{n=1}^∞ Λ(n) χ(n) e(δn/x) η(n/x)` becomes
  `∑' n : ℕ, Λ n * χ n * e (δ / x * n) * phiPos (n / x)` in `ℂ`. Here `e t = exp(2πit)`
  (`TernaryGoldbach.e`) and `Λ` is Mathlib's von Mangoldt function. The extra `n = 0` term is zero
  because `Λ 0 = 0`. The series converges absolutely (`prop_9_3_2_summable`), so the `tsum` is the
  true sum.
* `η̂` is Mathlib's Fourier transform `𝓕 f (w) = ∫ e(−vw) f(v) dv`. This is [H]'s normalization
  `f̂(t) = ∫ e(−xt) f(x) dx` (§2.3). `phiPos` is integrable, so this is the true integral.
* `O*(E) · x` means a quantity of absolute value at most `E · x`. The two cases of (9.56) become
  two implications joined by `∧`: `q = 1 → ‖Σ − η̂(−δ) x‖ ≤ err · x` and `1 < q → ‖Σ‖ ≤ err · x`.
* `err_{η,χ}(δ, x)` is `prop_9_3_2_err q T0 δ x`, i.e. (9.57).

1724.doc:
**[H, Proposition 7.1.5]**, as printed (p. 140).

How the statement is transcribed:
* `η = η₊` is the repository's `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.etaPlus`, `η₊(t) = h₂₀₀(t) · t · e^{−t²/2}`. We
  checked it against [H, (7.4)–(7.6)]:
  - `hBase` is the `h` of (7.5);
  - `F H y = sin(H log y)/(π log y)` is the `F_H` of (7.6). (7.6) writes `F_H(t)` and `(h *_M F_H)(y)`,
    typos for `F_H(y)` and `(h *_M F_H)(t)`; we read it as a function of `y`;
  - `hH H t = ∫_{y>0} h(t/y) F_H(y) dy/y`, an absolutely convergent integral for every `t`;
  - `H = 200` is fixed inside `etaPlus`.

  At `y = 1`, Lean's `F` takes the value `0/0 = 0` rather than the limit `H/π`. This is a single point
  and does not change the integral.
* "`x` a real number `≥ 10¹²`" becomes `∀ x : ℝ, 1e12 ≤ x → …`. Both displayed equalities are claimed
  for every such `x`, so they are joined by `∧`.
* `Σ_{n=1}^∞ Λ(n) (log n) η²(n/x)` becomes `∑' n : ℕ, Λ n * Real.log n * etaPlus (n / x) ^ 2`, reading
  `η²(n/x)` as `(η(n/x))²`. The extra `n = 0` term is zero because `Λ 0 = 0`. For every `x > 0` the
  series converges absolutely. Termwise it is `log x` times the series for `η₊²` plus the series for
  `η₊² log`, and both are absolutely convergent by `TernaryGoldbach.Explicit.summable_SsumG` (as used
  in `MajorArcs.prop_9_5_1`). So the `tsum` is the true sum.
* `∫₀^∞ η₊²(t) log x t dt` becomes `∫ t in Ioi 0, etaPlus t ^ 2 * Real.log (x * t)`. Here `log x t`
  means `log(xt)`, as in [H, §9.5], where `η₊²(t) log xt = (log x) η₊²(t) + η₊²(t) log t`. Both `η₊²`
  and `η₊² log` are integrable on `(0, ∞)` (shown in the proof of `MajorArcs.prop_9_5_1`), so the
  Bochner integral is the true integral.
* [H] defines `E₁` and `E₂` through the displayed equalities. Each becomes
  `∃ Eᵢ, |Eᵢ| ≤ bound ∧ equality`. Because `x log x > 0`, the equality determines `Eᵢ`, so this is [H]'s
  claim and not a weakening (see `prop_7_1_5_iff_bounds`). `Eᵢ · x log x` is written
  `Eᵢ * x * Real.log x`, as in the repository's `prop_7_1_5'`.
* The constants are copied verbatim: `0.640206`, `0.021095`, `5.123·10⁻¹⁵` (`5.123e-15`), `366.91`,
  `2·10⁻⁶` (`2e-6`). `√x` is `Real.sqrt x`.
* There is no hypothesis on zeros, on Platt's verification or on any other input, because the printed
  proposition is unconditional.

1974.doc:
`μ` is the Möbius function. If `n` is squarefree with an even number of distinct prime factors,
`μ n = 1`. If `n` is squarefree with an odd number of distinct prime factors, `μ n = -1`.
If `n` is not squarefree, `μ n = 0`.

20.doc:
The number π = 3.14159265... Defined here using choice as twice a zero of cos in [1,2],
from which one can derive all its properties. For explicit bounds on π,
see `Mathlib/Analysis/Real/Pi/Bounds.lean`.

Denoted `π`, once the `Real` namespace is opened.

2034.doc:
The book's constant `max_{q ≤ 2Q₀, q even} max_{s ≤ 2Q₀/q} G_q(2Q₀/sq)/G_q(2Q/sq)`, written as
the supremum of `ratioSet_12_1_2`. The set is finite and, for `Q₀ ≥ 1`, nonempty, so the supremum
is attained (`quotMax_12_1_2_isGreatest`): it is the book's maximum.

2035.doc:
**[H, Proposition 12.1.2]**, as printed (book p. 230).

Transcription:
* `x : ℝ` is the book's (implicit) real parameter; the hypotheses force `x ≥ 2`.
* The sequence `{aₙ}_{n ≥ 1}` is `a : ℕ → ℂ`; the extra value `a 0` is forced to be `0` by
  "supported on the primes", rendered `∀ n, a n ≠ 0 → n.Prime`.
* "`{aₙ}` is in `ℓ₁ ∩ ℓ₂`": `Summable (‖aₙ‖)` and `Summable (‖aₙ‖²)` (the second follows from the
  first; both are kept as printed).
* "`aₙ = 0` for `n ≤ √x`": `∀ n : ℕ, (n : ℝ) ≤ √x → a n = 0`.
* `Q₀ ≥ 1`, `δ₀ ≥ 1`, `δ₀ Q₀² ≤ x/2` verbatim. `Q = √(x/2δ₀)` is `√(x / (2 * δ₀))` (the proof
  uses `δ₀Q/(qx) = 1/(2qQ)`, i.e. `Q² = x/(2δ₀)`); the parenthetical "`≥ Q₀`" is a consequence
  (`le_sqrt_12_1_2`), not an extra hypothesis.
* `𝔐_{δ₀,Q₀} ⊂ ℝ/ℤ` is the book's (10.5) (`eq:majdef`): arcs `(a/q ∓ δ₀Q₀/(2qx))` for odd `q ≤ Q₀`
  and `(a/q ∓ δ₀Q₀/(qx))` for even `q ≤ 2Q₀`, `(a, q) = 1`. The repo's
  `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.majorArcs δ₀ Q₀ x` is exactly its preimage in `ℝ` (union over all
  integers `a` coprime to `q`, which is `1`-periodic), so the integral over `𝔐` for the Haar
  probability measure of `ℝ/ℤ` is the Lebesgue integral over `(0, 1] ∩ majorArcs δ₀ Q₀ x`.
* `S(α) = Σ aₙ e(αn)` is `TernaryGoldbach.expTsum a α = ∑' n, a n * e (n * α)` with
  `e t = exp(2πit)` (the book's `e`); `|S(α)|²` is `‖·‖ ^ 2` and `Σ |aₙ|²` is `∑' n, ‖a n‖ ^ 2`.
* The double maximum is `quotMax_12_1_2 x δ₀ Q₀` (see `ratioSet_12_1_2` for the range of `q, s`).
  Every denominator `G_q(2Q/sq)` is `≥ 1` on that range (`one_le_den_12_1_2`), so no division by
  zero occurs.

2259.doc:
**[H, Proposition 11.2.3]**, p. 223, as printed (both cases).

Transcription choices:
* `x, K` are real, with `1 ≤ K` and `K * 2.16e20 ≤ x` (`x ≥ K x₀`, `x₀ = 2.16·10²⁰`).
* `φ : [0, ∞) → [0, ∞)` continuous and in `L¹` becomes `φ : ℝ → ℝ` with `ContinuousOn φ (Ici 0)`,
  `∀ w ≥ 0, 0 ≤ φ w` and `IntegrableOn φ (Ici 0)`. The values of `φ` on `(−∞, 0)` never enter: the
  Mellin convolution at `t ≥ 0` evaluates `φ` at `t/w ≥ 0`, and all integrals are over subsets of
  `[0, ∞)`.
* `η_* = η₂ *_M φ` is `mellinConv eta2 φ`. The repository's `mellinConv f g t = ∫_{r>0} f(r) g(t/r) dr/r`
  is [H, (2.7)], and its `eta2 t = 4 max(log 2 − |log 2t|, 0)` (for `t > 0`, and `0` for `t ≤ 0`) is
  (11.10).
* `S_η(α, x)` is the repository's `S η x α = ∑' n, Λ(n) η(n/x) e(nα)`, which is (10.1); `α ∈ ℝ/ℤ` is
  represented by a real number (`e(nα)` is `1`-periodic in `α`). For `φ ∈ L¹` the series converges
  absolutely (`Σ Λ(n) η_*(n/x) = ∫ S_{η₂}(0, wx) φ(w) dw/w ≤ 1.04488 |φ|₁ x` by Tonelli and
  Cor. C.1.3), so the `tsum` is the genuine sum.
* `2α = a/q + δ/x` holds in `ℝ/ℤ`, so it becomes `∃ k : ℤ, 2 * α = a / q + δ / x + k`, with `a : ℤ`,
  `δ : ℝ` and `q : ℕ`, `0 < q` (implicit in [H]: `q` is a denominator). `gcd(a, q) = 1` is
  `Int.gcd a q = 1`; `Q = (3/4) x^{2/3}` is written out (`x ^ (2 / 3 : ℝ)`), and `1/qQ` means `1/(qQ)`.
* First case: the hypothesis `q ≤ (x/K)^{1/3}/6` and the conclusion
  `‖S_{η_*}(α, x)‖ ≤ g_{x,φ}(max(1, |δ|/8) q) · |φ|₁ · x`. (11.18) is printed without `|·|`, though
  `S` is complex; we read it as in the second case and as [H] uses it in (13.14)–(13.15). The
  refutation does not depend on this (`prop_11_2_3_counterexample_re`).
* `g_{x,φ}`, `R_{x,K,φ,t}`, `C_{φ,2,K}` are `prop_11_2_3_g`, `prop_11_2_3_RK`, `prop_11_2_3_C2`, copied
  from (11.19)–(11.20). Inside, the repository's `R x t` is `R_{x,t}`, its `Lg t` is `L_t` and its
  `Fr r` is `Ϝ(r) = e^γ log log r + 2.50637/log log r` ((11.13) and (C.19); we checked all three
  against [H]). `|φ|₁` is `prop_11_2_3_norm1 φ = ∫_{(0,∞)} |φ|`.
* Second case: the hypothesis `(x/K)^{1/3}/6 < q` and the conclusion
  `‖S_{η_*}(α, x)‖ ≤ h_φ(x/K) · |φ|₁ · x`, with `h_φ` and `C_{φ,0,K}` (`prop_11_2_3_hφ`,
  `prop_11_2_3_C0`) copied from (11.21) and `h` the repository's `hfun`, which is (11.15) verbatim.
* Both cases are claimed under the common hypotheses, so they are joined by `∧`.
* Degenerate inputs, where [H]'s right side is undefined and Lean substitutes junk values:
  - `K = 1`: `(R_{x/K,t} − R_{x,t}) (C_{φ,2,K}/|φ|₁)/log K` is `0 · (0/|φ|₁)/0`; Lean gives `0`, so
    `R_{x,1,φ,t} = R_{x,t}`, which is also the limit as `K → 1⁺` (`C_{φ,2,K} = O((log K)²)`).
  - `|φ|₁ = 0`: then `φ = 0` on `[0, ∞)`, `S_{η_*} = 0`, and both bounds read `0 ≤ 0`.
  - `1 ≤ r ≤ e` (possible only when `q ≤ 2`; [H]'s (11.11) assumes `q ≥ 3`): `log log r ≤ 0`, so
    `Ϝ(r)` is undefined or negative and `√Ϝ(r)` is undefined. Lean's conventions can make the bound
    negative there (e.g. `q = 1`, `|δ|` slightly above `8`), so the definition is also false at such
    points, for reasons that are not [H]'s. The refutation avoids them: it refutes the restriction
    `prop_11_2_3_first_case_nondegenerate`, on which no junk value occurs.

2530.doc:
`η̂₂''(t) = (2πit)² η̂₂(t)`: the Fourier transform of the distributional second derivative of
`η₂`, with the book's normalization. It is [H, §2.3]'s rule `f̂(t) = f̂'(t)/(2πit)`, applied twice.
The explicit form in [H]'s proof, `4g(t) + f̂(t)` from (B.7), is the same function
(`lemma_B_1_2_eta2DDhat_eq_measure`). It is `-eta2DD t` in the repository's notation
(`lemma_B_1_2_eta2DDhat_eq_neg_eta2DD`).

2531.doc:
**[H, Lemma B.1.2], equation (B.6), as printed**: `|η̂₂''|_∞ ≤ 31.521`.

Transcription choices:
* "`η₂ : ℝ⁺ → ℝ` as in (3.4)" is the repository's `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.eta2`. On
  `ℝ⁺ = (0, ∞)` it is the printed `4 max(log 2 - |log 2t|, 0)` (`lemma_B_1_2_eta2_of_pos`). On
  `(-∞, 0]` it is `0` (`lemma_B_1_2_eta2_of_nonpos`). Extending by zero is how [H] takes Fourier
  transforms of functions on `ℝ⁺` (`supp η₂ = (1/4, 1)`, [H, proof of Lemma B.2.1]).
* `η̂₂''` is `lemma_B_1_2_eta2DDhat`, that is `(2πit)² η̂₂(t)`, with the book's
  `f̂(t) = ∫ e(-xt) f(x) dx` (`lemma_B_1_2_hat`). `η₂'` jumps at `1/4`, `1/2` and `1`, so `η₂''`
  exists only as a distribution, and `(2πit)² η̂₂` is its Fourier transform. [H]'s explicit form
  `η̂₂''(t) = 4g(t) + f̂(t)` from (B.7) is the same function (`lemma_B_1_2_eta2DDhat_eq_measure`).
* "`|·|_∞ ≤ 31.521`" is `∀ t : ℝ, ‖η̂₂''(t)‖ ≤ 31.521`, for every real `t` of either sign. The
  bound is not written with `⨆`, whose junk value `0` for an unbounded family would make it
  vacuous. Reading `|·|_∞` as an essential supremum gives the same proposition
  (`lemma_B_1_2_iff_ae`). The literal `31.521` is the exact rational `31521/1000`.
* There are no hypotheses: the lemma is one numerical inequality.

2680.doc:
**[H, Lemma 4.1.3]**, p. 55, equation (4.6) and the sentence after it, as printed.

Transcription choices:
* The letters of the statement, `α, a, q, β, Q, y₁, y₂, B, C`, are universally quantified.
  `α, β, Q, y₁, y₂, B, C` are real, `a` is an integer, and `q` is a natural number with `0 < q`.
  [H] leaves `q ≥ 1` implicit, since `q` is the denominator of `a/q`.
* "Let `α = a/q + β/qQ`" becomes the hypothesis `α = a / q + β / (q * Q)`: in [H], `β/qQ` means
  `β/(qQ)`. `(a, q) = 1` becomes `Int.gcd a q = 1`. `|β| ≤ 1` and `q ≤ Q` are copied as they
  stand.
* "`y₂ > y₁ ≥ 0`" becomes `0 ≤ y₁` and `y₁ < y₂`. `y₂ - y₁ ≤ q` and `y₂ ≤ Q/2` are copied as
  they stand.
* `∑_{y₁ < n ≤ y₂, q ∤ n}` is the sum over the integers `n` in `(y₁, y₂]` with `q ∤ n`. It is
  written as the `Finset` sum over `Finset.Ioc ⌊y₁⌋ ⌊y₂⌋` filtered by `¬ (q : ℤ) ∣ n`, which is
  exactly that set (`lemma_4_1_3_mem_index`).
* The summand is copied as printed, `min (B / |sin (π α n)|) (C / |sin (π α n)| ^ 2)`. Under the
  hypotheses `sin (π α n) ≠ 0` for every `n` in the range (`lemma_4_1_3_sin_ne_zero`), so no
  division by zero occurs on the left.
* The right side of (4.6) is `2 * B * (q / π) * max 2 (log (C * exp 3 * q / (B * π)))`. Here
  `log` is the natural logarithm `Real.log`, and `e³ = Real.exp 3`.
* "The upper bound `≤ (2Bq/π) log(2e²q/π)` is also valid" holds under the same hypotheses. It is
  the second conjunct, `2 * B * q / π * log (2 * exp 2 * q / π)`.
* Degenerate inputs, where Lean's junk values replace expressions that [H] leaves undefined:
  - `B = 0`: [H]'s `Ce³q/(Bπ)` is undefined, and Lean reads it as `0`. The right side is then
    `0`, and so is the left side, since every term is `min 0 (C / sin²) = 0`. The bound reads
    `0 ≤ 0`.
  - `C = 0 < B`: [H]'s `log 0 = -∞` gives `max(2, log 0) = 2`. Lean's `Real.log 0 = 0` gives
    `max 2 0 = 2` as well.
  - In all other cases the argument of every `log` is positive, so no junk value appears.

The repository's definitions are not reused here: the statement involves only real arithmetic,
`sin`, `exp` and `log`.

2681.doc: A `with`-clause in a big operator. Example usage: `∑ i < 100 with Even i, f i`.

2730.doc:
**[H, (9.94)]** as printed (p. 197): for every real `x ≥ 10¹²`,
`∫₀^∞ η₊²(t) log xt dt = (0.640206 + O*(1.95·10⁻⁶)) log x − 0.021095 + O*(5.3·10⁻⁷)`.

Transcription choices.
* `η₊` is the repository's `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.etaPlus`, `η₊(t) = h₂₀₀(t) · t · e^{−t²/2}`.
  We checked it against [H, (7.4)–(7.6)] and against (9.63), "`η(t) = η₊(t) = h_H(t) · t e^{−t²/2}`,
  where `h_H` is as in (7.6)":
  - `hBase` is the `h` of (7.5): `t²(2 − t)³ e^{t−1/2}` on `[0, 2]`, `0` elsewhere;
  - `F H y` is `F_H(y) = sin(H log y)/(π log y)`;
  - `hH H t = ∫_{y>0} h(t/y) F_H(y) dy/y` is the `h_H(t)` of (7.6). (7.6) prints `F_H(t)` and
    `(h *_M F_H)(y)`, typos for `F_H(y)` and `(h *_M F_H)(t)`.

  `H = 200` is fixed inside `etaPlus`, as in §9.6 ("where, as before, `H = 200`", p. 196); the
  bound `274.86/H^{7/2}` just above (9.94) is also evaluated at `H = 200`. At `y = 1`, Lean's
  `F H 1` is `0/0 = 0` rather than the limit `H/π`. This changes the integrand defining `h_H` at
  one point only, so it does not change `h_H`.
* `η₊²(t)` is `etaPlus t ^ 2`. `log xt` is `Real.log (x * t)`, that is `log(xt)`. [H] reads it the
  same way in §9.5: "`η₊,₂ = (log x) η₊,₀ + η₊,₁ = η₊²(t) log xt`" (p. 189), where `η₊,₀ = η₊²` and
  `η₊,₁ = η₊² log t`.
* `∫₀^∞ … dt` is the Lebesgue (Bochner) integral over `Ioi 0`. The integrand is integrable for
  every `x > 0` (`eq_9_94_integrableOn`), so this is the true integral.
* `O*(R)` is "a quantity at most `R` in absolute value" ([H, §2.1]). The two `O*` terms become
  `∃ E₁ E₂, |E₁| ≤ 1.95·10⁻⁶ ∧ |E₂| ≤ 5.3·10⁻⁷ ∧ …`, quantified after `x`. This is the usual
  reading, in which they may depend on `x`; in fact they can be chosen independent of `x`
  (`eq_9_94_uniform`). As printed, `E₁` sits inside the coefficient of `log x`.
* The range: the display states none. The text around it assumes `x ≥ 10¹²` ("We make, again,
  the assumption `x ≥ 10¹²`", p. 197, used again on p. 198). This is the hypothesis of
  [H, Prop 7.1.5], the result being proved there. So `x` is a real number `≥ 10¹²`. The
  derivation itself only needs `log x ≥ 0`. The formal theorem covers `x ≥ 1`, and
  `eq_9_94_uniform` covers every `x > 0`.
* The constants are the printed decimals `0.640206`, `0.021095`, `1.95·10⁻⁶` (`1.95e-6`),
  `5.3·10⁻⁷` (`5.3e-7`) and `10¹²` (`1e12`), taken as exact real numbers.
* The display assumes nothing about the zeros of `ζ` or any other input, so the definition has no
  hypotheses either.

2789.doc:
The book's `H₂(S)` [H, (5.35)]: `(4/π²) G₂(S)` if `1 ≤ S < 16`, `0.15107` if `S ≥ 16`. The factor
`4/π²` is `6v/(π² σ(v))` at `v = 2`.

[H] prints the left side as `H₂(s)`, a typo for `H₂(S)`. It does not define `H₂` for `S < 1`. We use
`(4/π²) G₂(S)` there too, which is `0` by the book's remark `G₂(S) = 0` for `S < 1`. Only `[1, T]`
matters in (5.36). The repo's `H2` uses `max (T2 S) 0` instead of `G₂ S`. They agree because
`G₂ ≥ 0` (`H₂_eq`).

287.doc:
The book's one-sided Gaussian `η♥`: `η♥(t) = e^{-t²/2}` for `t ≥ 0` and `η♥(t) = 0` for `t < 0`
([H, §7.1]: "Write `η♥(t) = e^{-t²/2}`"; [H, §9.2, p. 177]: "we set `η♥(t) = 0` for `t < 0`"). It
takes the value `η♥(0) = 1`, as in [H]. A single point does not affect the Fourier transform.

288.doc: The real exponential function, defined as the real part of the complex exponential

289.doc:
The book's Fourier transform `f̂(t) = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} e(-xt) f(x) dx` ([H, §2.3], repeated after
Theorem 7.1.1), with `e(x) = e^{2πix}` (the repository's `TernaryGoldbach.e`). It is Mathlib's `𝓕`

2890.doc:
**[H, (5.36)] at `v = 2`, as printed**: for `T ≥ 1`, `∫₁ᵀ H₂(S) dS/S ≤ 0.15107 log T`.

Transcription:
* `H₂` is the book's `H₂` of (5.35) (`Eq_5_36.H₂`). It is built from the book's `G₂`, the exact
  triple sum (5.28) at `v = 2` (`Eq_5_36.G₂`; see their docstrings).
* `dS/S` is rendered as the integrand `H₂ S / S` of the interval integral `∫ S in 1..T`. `H₂/S` is
  integrable on `[1, T]` (`Eq_5_36.intervalIntegrable_H₂_div`), so this is the true integral.
* `0.15107` is the real literal. `log` is `Real.log`.
* The range of `T` is not printed. The integral starts at `1`, and [H, §6] uses (5.36) with
  `T = x/(U W₀) ≥ 1`, so we take `T ≥ 1`. The refutation does not depend on this choice: the bound
  fails at `T = 4` and at every `T ≥ 16` (`eq_5_36_fails_of_ge16`).
* Only `v = 2` is stated. The `v = 1` case (`0.22482 log T`) is not used by the formalization or by
  [H, Ch. 6], and is not transcribed.

291.doc:
**The remark after [H, Theorem 7.1.1]**, as printed (p. 138; also after (1.11)–(1.12), p. 14):
"`η̂♥(-δ)` is just `√(2π) e^{-2π²δ²}`".

How the statement is transcribed:
* `η♥` is the book's one-sided Gaussian `thm_7_1_1_etaHeart`, which is `0` on `(-∞, 0)`. This is
  the book's convention for its weights on `ℝ⁺` ([H, §9.2, p. 177], [H, Lemma 9.1.1] and its proof,
  p. 166), and the reading under which Theorem 7.1.1 can hold. Under the two-sided reading the
  remark is true (`thm_7_1_1_hat_gaussian`) and the theorem is false (`thm_7_1_1_twoSided_false`).
* `η̂` is `thm_7_1_1_hat`, with the book's normalization `f̂(t) = ∫ e(-xt) f(x) dx`, evaluated
  at `-δ`.
* The identity is claimed for every `δ ∈ ℝ`: the remark states a formula for the function
  `δ ↦ η̂♥(-δ)`. Restricting `δ` to the theorem's range `|δ| ≤ 4r/q` would not change the verdict,
  since `thm_7_1_1_remark_ne` refutes the identity at every single `δ`.
* `√(2π) e^{-2π²δ²}` is the real number `√(2 * π) * Real.exp (-2 * π ^ 2 * δ ^ 2)`, viewed in
  `ℂ`.

2921.doc:
`G_v(S)` of [H, p. 92], taken to be the triple sum [H, (5.28)]
`∑_{s ≤ S, (s,v)=1} (1/s) ∫_{1/2}^1 g_v(uS/s) du`.

Why this is the book's `G_v`. For `S < 100000` the book computes `G_v` "using the exact expression
(5.29) instead of (5.30)". (5.29) is the exact coefficient of `g_v(m)` in (5.28), so summing it
over `m ≤ S` gives (5.28) itself, in the form `K_{v,1}(⌊S⌋) + K_{v,2}(⌊S⌋)/S` that the book
describes (`eq_5_32_G_eq`). We read the printed `K_{v,1}(|S|)` as `K_{v,1}(⌊S⌋)`, since the
previous sentence says the coefficients depend only on `⌊S⌋`. The book calls `G_v` "a bound of the
form", perhaps because it was computed with upward rounding. `eq_5_32_v2_majorant_fails` and
`eq_5_32_v1_majorant_fails` show that the refutation holds for every such bound. This `G_v`
reproduces the book's example, `1 − 1/S` on `[1, 2)` and `0` for `S < 1` (`eq_5_32_G_lt_two`,
`eq_5_32_G_lt_one`). For `v = 2` it is the repository's `T2` (`eq_5_32_G_two`).

2922.doc:
**[H, (5.32)]** as printed:
`∫₁ᵀ G_v(S) dS/S ≤ 0.3698 log T` if `v = 1`, and `≤ 0.37273 log T` if `v = 2`.

Transcription choices:
* `G_v` is `eq_5_32_G v` (see there).
* `∫₁ᵀ … dS/S` is the interval integral `∫ S in 1..T, G_v(S) / S`. On `[1, T]` the integrand is
  bounded and measurable, so this is the ordinary integral. Integrability on `[1, 4]` and
  `[1, 5]` is proved explicitly (`eq_5_32_v2_integral_four`, `eq_5_32_v1_integral_five`), so the
  refutation is not an artefact of Lean's convention that a non-integrable function has
  integral `0`.
* The display gives no range for `T`. We take every `T ≥ 1`, because the integral starts at `1`,
  and for `0 < T < 1` the right-hand side is negative while the left-hand side is `0`. The book's
  numerical check covers `T ∈ [2, 40]`. Its use in (5.36) needs `[1, 40]` for `v = 1` and
  `[1, 16]` for `v = 2`. The counterexamples `T = 5` (`v = 1`) and `T = 4` (`v = 2`) lie in every
  one of these ranges.
* The two cases are joined by `∧`. The constants `0.3698` and `0.37273` are as printed.

297.doc: `Ioi a` is the left-open right-infinite interval $(a, ∞)$.

31.doc:
The conclusion of [H, Theorem 7.1.4] for given `x`, `q`, `χ`, `δ`:
`Σ_{n=1}^∞ Λ(n) χ(n) e(δn/x) η(n/x) = I_{q=1} · η̂(−δ) · x + E · x` with
`|E| ≤ 1.3482·10⁻¹⁴ + 1.617·10⁻¹⁰/q + (1/√x)(499900/√q + 52)`, and also
`|E| ≤ 4.772·10⁻¹¹ + 251400/√x` if `q = 1`.

How it is transcribed:
* The series is `∑' n : ℕ+` (that is, `n = 1, 2, …`) of `Λ(n) χ(n) e(δ/x · n) η₊(n/x)`. Here `Λ`
  is Mathlib's `ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt`, `e(u) = exp(2πiu)` is `TernaryGoldbach.e` and
  `χ(n)` is `χ (n : ZMod q)`. The series converges absolutely (`Thm_7_1_4.summable_norm`), so the
  `tsum` is its sum. It is the repository's `Schar χ (n ↦ Λ(n) η₊(n/x)) (δ/x)`
  (`Thm_7_1_4.sum_eq_Schar`).
* `η̂` is `Thm_7_1_4.fourierHat`, the normalization `f̂(t) = ∫ e(−xt) f(x) dx` of [H, §2.3],
  evaluated at `−δ`. Its integrand is integrable (`Thm_7_1_4.integrable_integrand`).
* `I_{q=1}` is `if q = 1 then 1 else 0`.
* [H] defines `E` through the identity, so `E` becomes `∃ E : ℂ, identity ∧ ‖E‖ ≤ …`. `E` is
  complex, because the sum is, and `|E|` is its modulus `‖E‖`. Since `x > 0`, the identity
  determines `E`, so this is [H]'s claim and not a weakening (`thm_7_1_4_concl_iff`). The sharper
  `q = 1` bound is the clause `q = 1 → ‖E‖ ≤ …` on the same `E`.
* The constants are copied verbatim: `1.3482e-14`, `1.617e-10`, `499900`, `52`, `4.772e-11`,
  `251400`. `√` is `Real.sqrt`.
31.signature: Companion.Book.thm_7_1_4_concl (x : ℝ) (q : ℕ) (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ q) (δ : ℝ) : Prop

3137.doc:
The book's triple sum [H, (5.28), p. 89], the left side of (5.31):
`T_v(S) = ∑_{s ≤ S, (s,v)=1} (1/s) ∫_{1/2}^1 g_v(uS/s) du`.

Transcription: `s` runs over the positive integers `≤ S` (`Finset.Icc 1 ⌊S⌋₊`) with
`(s, v) = 1`. The integral is the interval integral over `[1/2, 1]`. The integrand is a step
function of `u`, so it agrees with the book's Riemann integral. At `v = 2` this is the repo's
`TernaryGoldbach.MinorArcs.T2` (`TBook_two`).

3138.doc:
**[H, (5.31)]** as printed (p. 91, with its range extension on p. 92):
`T_1(S) ≤ 0.36393` for `S ≥ 40`, and `T_2(S) ≤ 0.37273` for `S ≥ 16`.

Transcription choices.
* Both cases of the display are kept: `v = 1` (constant `0.36393`) and `v = 2` (constant
  `0.37273`). The constants are exactly the printed decimals, as real numbers.
* The ranges: the display is introduced by "Thus, for `S ≥ 100000`". The next paragraph says it
  also holds for `40 ≤ S < 100000` if `v = 1` and for `16 ≤ S < 100000` if `v = 2`. Taken
  together, the book claims (5.31) for `S ≥ 40` (`v = 1`) and `S ≥ 16` (`v = 2`). This is what
  is stated here. `eq_5_31_iff_as_printed` proves it equivalent to the conjunction of the two
  printed clauses, each rendered literally.
* `S` is a real number (in [H] it is `x/(WU)`). `T_v` is the book's object `TBook` (with
  `gBook`), not the repo's `T2`. `TBook 2 = T2` is a theorem here (`TBook_two`), and `TBook 1`
  has no counterpart in the repo.

3177.doc:
**[H, (2.21)] as printed** (Ramaré): for `x ≥ 11815`,
`|∑_{n ≤ x} μ(n)/n| ≤ 0.03/log x`.

Transcription choices:
* `x` is a real number: the book's `x` in §2.5 is real ((2.24) is stated "for all real
  `x ≤ 10¹²`"), and [H] applies (2.21) at real arguments ((5.26)). Writing
  `m(N) = ∑_{n ≤ N} μ(n)/n`, the bound must then hold on each whole interval `[N, N + 1)`, i.e.
  `|m(N)| ≤ 0.03/log(N + 1)` for every integer `N ≥ 11815`; this is stronger than the reading with
  `x` an integer (`|m(N)| ≤ 0.03/log N`).
* The range `x ≥ 11815` is the hypothesis `11815 ≤ x`.
* `∑_{n ≤ x}` ranges over the *positive* integers `n ≤ x` ([H, §2.1]: `∑_n` means `∑_{n=1}^∞`).
  It is written literally as the `finsum` over `{n : ℕ | 1 ≤ n ∧ (n : ℝ) ≤ x}`, with the comparison
  `n ≤ x` made in `ℝ` (no floor). This set is finite, so the `finsum` is the genuine finite sum
  (`eq_2_21_finsum_eq_sum_Icc`).
* `μ` is Mathlib's `ArithmeticFunction.moebius` (`ℤ`-valued, cast to `ℝ`), which agrees with the
  book's definition on positive integers (`eq_2_21_moebius_eq_book`,
  `eq_2_21_book_moebius_unique`); `μ(n)/n` is the real quotient `(μ n : ℝ) / (n : ℝ)`.
* `log` is the natural logarithm `Real.log` (positive for `x ≥ 11815`); `0.03` is the real number
  `3/100`; `|·|` is the real absolute value.

3229.doc:
**[H, (14.7)]** as printed (p. 261). For every real `x ≥ x₊ = 4.9·10²⁶`,
`∫_{𝔐_{8,r₀}} |S_{η₊}(α,x)|² dα = (8.70524 + O*(0.00007)) x + O*(0.075273) x
= (8.7052 + O*(0.0754)) x ≤ 8.7806 x`.

How the statement is transcribed:
* **Range.** (14.7) prints no range of its own. The preamble of Ch. 14 fixes `x₊ = 4.9·10²⁶` and
  says the results must hold for every `x ≥ x₊`. The inputs of (14.7) are stated for that range:
  (14.1) is evaluated at `x₊`, and the bound on `K_{r,2}` is stated "for `x ≥ x₊`". So the range
  becomes `∀ x : ℝ, 4.9e26 ≤ x → …`, with `x` real. (In §14.4, `x = N/(2 + 9/(196√(2π)))`.)
* **Parameters.** `δ₀ = 8`: §14.1 says "Recall that `δ₀ = 8`". `r₀ = 150000`: the Ch. 14 preamble
  fixes `r = 150000`, (14.7) writes it as the subscript `r₀`, and §14.3 restates `r₀ = 150000`.
  So `𝔐_{8,r₀}` is `majorArcs 8 r₀ x`, with `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.r₀ = 150000`.
* **Major arcs.** `𝔐_{δ₀,r}` is the subset of `ℝ/ℤ` defined in (10.5). It is the union, over
  `a mod q` with `(a,q) = 1`, of the arcs `(a/q − δ₀r/(2qx), a/q + δ₀r/(2qx))` for odd `q ≤ r` and
  `(a/q − δ₀r/(qx), a/q + δ₀r/(qx))` for even `q ≤ 2r`. `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.majorArcs δ₀ r x`
  is the same union lifted to `ℝ`: `q ≥ 1` and all `a ∈ ℤ` with `IsCoprime a q`, which over `ℤ`
  means `gcd(a,q) = 1`. That is exactly the preimage of [H]'s set under `ℝ → ℝ/ℤ`. The arcs use
  the same `x` as `S_{η₊}(α,x)`, as in (10.5) and Lemma 10.3.1.
* **The integral.** [H]'s `∫_{𝔐} … dα` is over `ℝ/ℤ` with its Haar probability measure. It becomes
  `∫ α in Set.Ioc 0 1 ∩ majorArcs 8 r₀ x` with Lebesgue measure. This works because `(0,1]` is a
  fundamental domain and both the integrand and the lifted arcs are `1`-periodic
  (`eq_14_7_S_add_one`, `eq_14_7_majorArcs_add_one`). The integrand is continuous, hence
  integrable on this set (`eq_14_7_integrableOn`), so the Bochner integral is [H]'s integral.
  This is the same set expression as in `l2_major_bounds`.
* **Exponential sum.** (10.1) defines `S_η(α,x) = Σ_n Λ(n) e(αn) η(n/x)`. This is
  `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.S η x α` (note the argument order), the series
  `∑' n : ℕ, Λ(n) η(n/x) e(nα)` with `e(t) = exp(2πit)`. The extra `n = 0` term is zero because
  `Λ 0 = 0`. For `x > 0` the series converges absolutely
  (`TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.summable_etaPlus`), so the `tsum` is the true sum. `|S|²` is written
  `‖S etaPlus x α‖ ^ 2`.
* **Smoothing.** [H] defines `η₊(t) = h₂₀₀(t) t e^{−t²/2}`, with `h_H(t) = ∫₀^∞ h(t/y) F_H(y) dy/y`,
  `h(t) = t²(2−t)³ e^{t−1/2}` on `[0,2]` (zero elsewhere) and `F_H(y) = sin(H log y)/(π log y)`
  ((7.4)–(7.6), restated in the Ch. 14 preamble; both print `F_H(t)` on the left of a formula in
  `y`, which we read as `F_H(y)`). `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.etaPlus` matches this
  definition for definition (`hBase`, `F`, `hH`, with `H = 200`). At `y = 1`, Lean's `F` takes the
  value `0/0 = 0` instead of the limit `H/π`. This is a single point and does not change the
  integral.
* **`O*`.** `O*(c)` stands for a quantity of absolute value at most `c`. Each `O*` becomes an
  existential `E` with `|E| ≤ c`. The first member has two of them: `E₁` in the main-term constant
  `8.70524 + O*(0.00007)` (that is, `L_{r,δ₀}`) and `E₂` in the error term `O*(0.075273) x`.
  Because `x > 0`, these existentials amount to explicit two-sided bounds (`eq_14_7_iff_bounds`).
* **The chain.** Each of the three members is asserted of the integral, and the three claims are
  joined by `∧`. The first claim implies the other two (`eq_14_7_iff_line1`).
* **Constants.** They are copied verbatim: `8.70524`, `0.00007`, `0.075273`, `8.7052`, `0.0754`,
  `8.7806`.
* **No hypotheses.** (14.7) is stated unconditionally ([H] treats Platt's GRH verification as a
  theorem), so the definition has no hypotheses. The formalization's `Fact` hypotheses appear only
  in `eq_14_7_holds`.

33.doc:
The natural numbers, starting at zero.

This type is special-cased by both the kernel and the compiler, and overridden with an efficient
implementation. Both use a fast arbitrary-precision arithmetic library (usually
[GMP](https://gmplib.org/)); at runtime, `Nat` values that are sufficiently small are unboxed.

3375.doc:
**`|η|_∞`**, the sup norm on `[0, ∞)`: `sup_{t ≥ 0} |η(t)|`.

[H, §2.1] writes `|f|_r` for the `L_r` norm; the repo has no sup-norm object. The domain
`[0, ∞)` is where `η₊` and `η_*` live: Thm. 13.2.1, which the Ch. 14 preamble cites, takes
`η₊` and `φ` on `[0, ∞)`, and `η_*` is a Mellin convolution, defined for `t ≥ 0`. The rest of
this paragraph consists of mathematical remarks: they are not proved here, and no proof in this
file needs them. `η₊` vanishes on `(-∞, 0]` (`h₂₀₀(t) = 0` for `t < 0`, since `h` is supported
on `[0, 2]`). The repo's `etaStar` uses the Mellin-convolution formula for every `t ∈ ℝ`, and it
is even in `t` because `φ` is, so the supremum over `ℝ` is the same. Both functions are
continuous on `[0, ∞)`, so their `L_∞` norm equals this pointwise supremum (the repo has no
continuity lemma for `etaPlus` or `etaStar`).

The pointwise supremum is in any case the reading the first inequality of (14.51) needs, since it
bounds the values `|η₊(nᵢ/x)|` and `|η_*(n₃/x)|` one by one.

Lean's `⨆` returns `0` for a family that is not bounded above. Both functions are bounded on
`[0, ∞)` (`eq_14_51_supNorm_etaPlus_le`, `eq_14_51_supNorm_etaStar_le`), so here it is the true
supremum (`eq_14_51_le_supNorm`).

3377.doc:
**The first member of (14.51)** ("the sum on the first line of (14.51)"):
`∑_{n₁+n₂+n₃=N, n₁, n₂ or n₃ even or non-prime} Λ(n₁)Λ(n₂)Λ(n₃) η₊(n₁/x) η₊(n₂/x) η_*(n₃/x)`
with `x = xOf N = N/(2 + 9/(196√(2π)))` [H, (14.15)].

The `nᵢ` are positive integers ([H, §2.1]: `∑_n` means `∑_{n ≥ 1}`). A triple with
`n₁ + n₂ + n₃ = N` has every `nᵢ ∈ [1, N]`, so the book's finite sum is the triple sum over
`Icc 1 N` cut down by the `if`. "`n₁, n₂ or n₃` even or non-prime" means that at least one `nᵢ`
is even or not prime. This is the complement of "`n₁, n₂, n₃` odd primes" in the last display of
§14.4.

3378.doc:
**The sum in the second member of (14.51)**:
`∑_{n₁+n₂+n₃=N, n₁ even or non-prime} Λ(n₁)Λ(n₂)Λ(n₃)`, unweighted, over positive integers as in
`eq_14_51_first`.

3379.doc:
**The third member of (14.51) without the factor `3 |η₊|²_∞ |η_*|_∞`**:
`(log N) ∑_{n₁ ≤ N non-prime or n₁ = 2} Λ(n₁) ∑_{n₂ ≤ N} Λ(n₂)`, with `n₁, n₂ ≥ 1` and the
natural logarithm.

3380.doc:
**[H, (14.51)]** as printed: for every natural number `N ≥ 10²⁷`, with
`x = N/(2 + 9/(196√(2π)))`,

`∑_{n₁+n₂+n₃=N, n₁, n₂ or n₃ even or non-prime} Λ(n₁)Λ(n₂)Λ(n₃) η₊(n₁) η₊(n₂) η_*(n₃)`
`  ≤ 3 |η₊|²_∞ |η_*|_∞ ∑_{n₁+n₂+n₃=N, n₁ even or non-prime} Λ(n₁)Λ(n₂)Λ(n₃)`
`  ≤ 3 |η₊|²_∞ |η_*|_∞ · (log N) ∑_{n₁ ≤ N non-prime or n₁ = 2} Λ(n₁) ∑_{n₂ ≤ N} Λ(n₂)`.

Transcription choices.
* The chain `A ≤ B ≤ C` is the conjunction `A ≤ B ∧ B ≤ C`. The members are `eq_14_51_first`,
  `eq_14_51_second` and `eq_14_51_third`, each multiplied by the constant
  `3 |η₊|²_∞ |η_*|_∞ = 3 * eq_14_51_supNorm etaPlus ^ 2 * eq_14_51_supNorm etaStar` where the
  book has it.
* Range: `N` is a natural number with `N ≥ 10²⁷`, the standing assumption of Ch. 14 (preamble:
  "we want a result valid for `N ≥ 10²⁷`"; after (14.15): "since we are assuming `N ≥ 10²⁷`").
  (14.51) is introduced by "Clearly" with no parity hypothesis. §14.4 assumes "`N` odd" in the
  display before (14.51), for the arcs, and again in the final display after it. (14.51) itself
  never uses parity. The chain holds for every `N ≥ 1` (`eq_14_51_chain`), so the reading "odd
  `N ≥ 10²⁷`" is covered too.
* The book prints `η₊(n₁) η₊(n₂) η_*(n₃)`, an abbreviation for `η₊(n₁/x) η₊(n₂/x) η_*(n₃/x)`.
  That is forced by (10.2), which writes `ηᵢ(nᵢ/x)`, and by (14.50), which equates this sum with
  `∫ S_{η₊}(α,x)² S_{η_*}(α,x) e(-Nα) dα`, where `S_η(α,x) = ∑ Λ(n) e(αn) η(n/x)`. Here
  `x = TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.xOf N = N/(2 + 9/(196√(2π)))`, which is [H, (14.15)]
  (`N/(2 + c₁/κ)` with `c₁/κ = (9/4)/(49√(2π))`).
* `η₊(t) = h₂₀₀(t) t e^{-t²/2}` (Ch. 14 preamble, [H, (7.4)–(7.6)]) is
  `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.etaPlus`, definition for definition. `η_*(t) = (η₂ *_M φ)(κt)`,
  `φ(t) = t² e^{-t²/2}`, `κ = 49`, `η₂ = η₁ *_M η₁` is `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.etaStar`, with
  `η₁ = 2·1_{[1/2,1]}` as in (11.10). The preamble's `2·1_{[-1/2,1/2]}` is a misprint, see
  `Companion/Book/Eq_14_49.lean`. (14.21)'s `|η₂(t)/t|₁ = 4(log 2)²` also requires (11.10)'s
  `η₁`.
* `|η|_∞` is `eq_14_51_supNorm`, the supremum of `|η|` over `[0, ∞)` (see its docstring).
* The sums run over positive integers. The condition "`n₁` even or non-prime" is
  `Even n₁ ∨ ¬ n₁.Prime`. "`n₁ ≤ N` non-prime or `n₁ = 2`" is `1 ≤ n₁ ≤ N` with
  `¬ n₁.Prime ∨ n₁ = 2`. `log` is `Real.log`.

Non-vacuity: the sup norms are genuine suprema of bounded functions (`eq_14_51_le_supNorm`), not
Lean's junk value `0`, and the first member is the repo's `repSum` difference
(`eq_14_51_first_eq`). Proved: `eq_14_51_holds`.

3571.doc:
**[H, (14.49)]** as printed, first member against last member:
for `r₀ = 150000` and every real `x ≥ 4.9·10²⁶`,
`Z_{r₀} = ∫_{(ℝ/ℤ) \ 𝔐_{8,r₀}} |S_{η_*}(α,x)| |S_{η₊}(α,x)|² dα ≤ 1.00948 x²/κ`.

Transcription choices.
* `x` is a real number with `x ≥ 4.9·10²⁶` (`x₊` of the Ch. 14 preamble; Theorem 13.2.1 asks for
  `x ≥ 10²⁵ κ`, the same number). (14.49) does not involve `N`.
* `S_η(α,x) = ∑ₙ Λ(n) e(αn) η(n/x)` ([H, (10.1)], (13.9)) is `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.S`, a
  `tsum` over `ℕ` (`Λ(0) = 0`); for `η₊`, `η_*` and `x > 0` the series is absolutely summable
  (`summable_etaPlus`, `summable_etaStar`), so the `tsum` is the book's sum.
* `η₊(t) = h₂₀₀(t) t e^{-t²/2}`, `h_H(t) = ∫₀^∞ h(t/y) F_H(y) dy/y`, `h(t) = t²(2-t)³e^{t-1/2}`
  on `[0,2]` (`0` elsewhere), `F_H(y) = sin(H log y)/(π log y)` ([H, (7.4)–(7.6)], Ch. 14
  preamble, `H = 200`) is `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.etaPlus`, definition for definition
  (`hBase`, `F`, `hH`).
* `η_*(t) = (η₂ *_M φ)(κt)` with `φ(t) = t² e^{-t²/2}`, `κ = 49`,
  `η₂ = η₁ *_M η₁ = 4 max(log 2 - |log 2t|, 0)`, `η₁ = 2·1_{[1/2,1]}` ([H, (11.10)], which
  Theorem 13.2.1 cites) is `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.etaStar` (`mellinConv eta2 phi (κ * t)`, with
  `(f *_M g)(t) = ∫₀^∞ f(r) g(t/r) dr/r` as in [H, (2.7)]). The Ch. 14 preamble prints
  `η₁ = 2·1_{[-1/2,1/2]}`, a misprint for (11.10)'s `2·1_{[1/2,1]}` (a Mellin convolution only
  sees `(0,∞)`, and Theorem 13.2.1 refers to (11.10)); we follow (11.10).
* `𝔐_{8,r₀}` is (10.5) with `δ₀ = 8`, `r = r₀ = 150000`, defined with the same `x` as in
  `S_η(α,x)`: arcs of radius `δ₀r/(2qx)` around `a/q` for odd `q ≤ r` and of radius `δ₀r/(qx)`
  for even `q ≤ 2r`, `(a,q) = 1`. `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.majorArcs 8 r₀ x` is exactly this,
  lifted to `ℝ` (all `a ∈ ℤ` coprime to `q`, i.e. the preimage of the book's subset of `ℝ/ℤ`).
  Reading chosen: the arcs are at scale `x`, as (10.5) and Theorem 13.2.1's "`𝔐_{δ₀,r}` as in
  (10.5) with `δ₀ = 8`" literally say, and as §14.4 needs (the minor arcs must be the complement
  of the major arcs of (14.27), which are at scale `x`). The proof of Theorem 13.2.1 uses arcs at
  scale `x/κ` for its ℓ∞ input (repo `NOTES.md`, "Ch. 13: scale erratum"); that concerns the
  proof, not the printed statement. (With arcs at scale `x/κ` the minor arcs would be smaller and
  the statement would no longer imply the formal one.)
* `∫_{(ℝ/ℤ) \ 𝔐}` (Haar probability measure) is written `∫ α in (0,1] \ majorArcs 8 r₀ x`
  (Lebesgue measure): `(0,1]` is a fundamental domain, and the lifted arcs
  (`eq_14_49_majorArcs_add_one`) and the integrand (`eq_14_49_S_add_one`) are `1`-periodic. The
  integrand is integrable there (`eq_14_49_integrableOn`), so Lean's Bochner integral is the
  book's integral.
* `|S_{η_*}(α,x)| |S_{η₊}(α,x)|²` is `‖S etaStar x α‖ * ‖S etaPlus x α‖ ^ 2`, in the book's order.
* `1.00948 x²/κ` is `1.00948 * x ^ 2 / κ` with `κ = TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.κ = 49`.
* Only the end-to-end inequality is transcribed: the intermediate members involve the
  quantities `M`, `T`, `E`, `S_{η_*}(0,x)` of Theorem 13.2.1 and §14.3, which are separate items;
  the last step of the chain is checked in `eq_14_49_last_step`.

36.doc:
The universe of propositions. `Prop ≡ Sort 0`.

Every proposition is propositionally equal to either `True` or `False`.

3603.doc:
**[H, (14.27)]** as printed: for `δ₀ = 8`, `r = r₀ = 150000`, `κ = 49`, every odd `N` and
every real `x ≥ x₊ = 4.9·10²⁶` with `x = N/(2 + c₁/κ)`, `c₁ = (9/4)/√(2π)`,
`∫_{𝔐_{8,r}} S_{η₊}(α,x)² S_{η_*}(α,x) e(−Nα) dα ≥ (1.058259/κ) x²`.

Transcription choices.
* `N : ℕ` odd: §14.2 bounds `C₀` (14.8) using only that `2 ∤ N` ("the only prime that we know
  does not divide `N` is `2`", (14.9)).
* `x : ℝ` with `x = N/(2 + c₁/κ)`, `c₁ = (9/4)/√(2π)`: (14.15) ("We have finally chosen `x` in
  terms of `N`"), written `x = N / (2 + 9 / 4 / √(2 * Real.pi) / κ)`; the lower bound (14.14) on
  `C_{η∘,η_*}` is computed for exactly this `N/x = 2 + c₁/κ`.
* `x ≥ 4.9·10²⁶`: the derivation of (14.26)–(14.27) invokes "the assumption `x ≥ x₊`" with
  `x₊ = 4.9·10²⁶` (Ch. 14 preamble: "Our results will have to be valid for any `x ≥ x₊`").
  Reading chosen: this, rather than the chapter's standing assumption `N ≥ 10²⁷` from which
  (14.16) deduces `x ≥ x₊`. The other reading is `eq_14_27_N`; `eq_14_27` implies it
  (`eq_14_27_implies_N`), and it also implies `major_arcs_input`.
* `S_η(α,x) = ∑ₙ Λ(n) e(αn) η(n/x)` (10.1) is `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.S`, a `tsum` over `ℕ`
  (`Λ(0) = 0`); for `η₊`, `η_*` and `x > 0` the series is absolutely summable
  (`summable_etaPlus`, `summable_etaStar`), so the `tsum` is the book's sum.
  `e(t) = exp(2πit)` is `TernaryGoldbach.e`.
* `η₊(t) = h₂₀₀(t) t e^{−t²/2}`, `h_H(t) = ∫₀^∞ h(t/y) F_H(y) dy/y`,
  `h(t) = t²(2−t)³e^{t−1/2}` on `[0,2]` (`0` elsewhere), `F_H(y) = sin(H log y)/(π log y)`
  (Ch. 14 preamble, `H = 200`) is `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.etaPlus`, definition for definition
  (`hBase`, `F`, `hH`; Lean's `F H 1 = 0` is a single point and does not affect `h_H`).
* `η_*(t) = (η₂ *_M φ)(κt)`, `φ(t) = t² e^{−t²/2}`, with the Mellin convolution (2.7)
  `(f *_M g)(t) = ∫₀^∞ f(w) g(t/w) dw/w`, is `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.etaStar`
  (`mellinConv eta2 phi (κ * t)`), with `η₂ = η₁ *_M η₁ = 4 max(log 2 − |log 2t|, 0)`,
  `η₁ = 2·1_{[1/2,1]}` as in (11.10). The Ch. 14 preamble prints `η₁ = 2·1_{[−1/2,1/2]}`, a
  misprint (a Mellin convolution only sees `(0,∞)`, and §14.2 uses that `η₂` is supported in
  `[1/4,1]`, which holds for (11.10)'s `η₂` but not for the printed one); we follow (11.10).
* `𝔐_{8,r}` is (10.5) with `δ₀ = 8`, `r = 150000`, at the same scale `x` as `S_η(α,x)`: arcs of
  radius `δ₀r/(2qx)` around `a/q` for odd `q ≤ r` and `δ₀r/(qx)` for even `q ≤ 2r`, `(a,q) = 1`.
  `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.majorArcs 8 r₀ x` is this set lifted to `ℝ` (all `a ∈ ℤ` coprime to
  `q`: the preimage of the book's subset of `ℝ/ℤ`).
* `∫_{𝔐_{8,r}} … dα` over `ℝ/ℤ` (Haar probability measure) is
  `∫ α in (0,1] ∩ majorArcs 8 r₀ x, …` (Lebesgue measure): `(0,1]` is a fundamental domain, and
  the lifted arcs (`eq_14_27_majorArcs_add_one`) and the integrand (`eq_14_27_S_add_one`) are
  `1`-periodic. The integrand is integrable there (`eq_14_27_integrableOn`).
* The integrand `S_{η₊}(α,x)² S_{η_*}(α,x) e(−Nα)` is
  `S etaPlus x α ^ 2 * S etaStar x α * TernaryGoldbach.e (-(N * α))`, literally the body of the
  repo's `TernaryGoldbach.MajorArcs.fI N x α`.
* "`≥`" between the complex-valued integral and a real number is read on the real part. This is
  no loss: the integral is real (`eq_14_27_integral_im_eq_zero`), and `eq_14_27_iff_complex_le`
  proves `eq_14_27` equivalent to the literal statement in `ℂ`'s partial order.
* `(1.058259/κ) x²` is `1.058259 / κ * x ^ 2` with `κ = TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.κ = 49`.

3697.doc:
[H, (12.14)]: `c_E = γ + ∑_{p ≥ 2} log p/(p(p−1))`, transcribed literally. `γ` is Mathlib's
`Real.eulerMascheroniConstant`, and the sum runs over the type `Nat.Primes` of all primes. It equals
the repo's `Prelim.RamPf.cR` (`eq_12_12_cE_eq`). The series is summable (`eq_12_12_cE_summable`),
so the `tsum` is the genuine sum. `Prelim.RamPf.cR_bounds` gives `1.3325822 ≤ c_E ≤ 1.3325823`,
which matches the printed `1.3325822…` and [Ram95, (3.6)] `1.33258227533221…`.

3700.doc:
[H, (12.13)]: `f₁(d) = ∏_{p ∣ d} (1 + p^{−2/3}) (1 + (p^{1/3} + p^{2/3})/(p(p−1)))^{−1}`,
transcribed literally, with the printed `(·)^{−1}`. The product runs over the prime divisors of
`d`, i.e. over `d.primeFactors` (for `d ≥ 1`, `p ∈ d.primeFactors ↔ p prime ∧ p ∣ d`).
The powers are real powers `Real.rpow` of `(p : ℝ) > 0`. It equals the repo's `Prelim.f1qP`
(`eq_12_12_f1_eq`), which writes the inverse as a division.

3701.doc:
**[H, (12.12)] as printed** (= [Ram95, Lemma 3.4] restricted to `R ≥ 1`): for every positive
integer `d` and every real `R ≥ 1`,
`G_d(R) = (φ(d)/d)(log R + c_E + ∑_{p ∣ d} log p/p) + O*(7.284 R^{−1/3} f₁(d))`.

Transcription choices:
* `d ∈ ℤ⁺` is `d : ℕ` with `1 ≤ d`; `R` is real with `1 ≤ R`, as printed.
* `O*(7.284 R^{−1/3} f₁(d))` is read as "`|G_d(R) − main term| ≤ 7.284 R^{−1/3} f₁(d)`". The
  bound is a product of nonnegative reals, and `R^{−1/3}` is `R ^ (-(1/3 : ℝ))` (real power, `R > 0`).
* `G_d(R)` is the repo's `Prelim.GqP d R`, which is [H, (12.2)] (`eq_12_12_GqP_eq`, by `rfl`): the
  sum over `r ∈ [1, ⌊R⌋₊]` with `Nat.Coprime r d` of `μ(r)²/φ(r)`. That is the sum over the positive
  integers `r ≤ R` with `(r, d) = 1`, with Mathlib's `μ` and `φ` (real division).
* `φ(d)/d` is the real quotient `(φ d : ℝ) / d`; `log` is `Real.log`.
* `∑_{p ∣ d} log p/p` is written inline as a sum over `d.primeFactors`. It is the repo's
  `Prelim.SqP d` by definition (`eq_12_12_SqP_eq`).
* `c_E` is `eq_12_12_cE` ((12.14), literal) and `f₁` is `eq_12_12_f1` ((12.13), literal).

39.doc:
`ℕ+` is the type of positive natural numbers. It is defined as a subtype,
and the VM representation of `ℕ+` is the same as `ℕ` because the proof
is not stored.

3928.doc:
The book's `η(t) = t² e^{-t²/2} *_M η₂(t)`, with the factors in the printed order. It is defined
on all of `ℝ` by the convolution formula and vanishes on `(-∞, 0]` (`cor_7_1_3_eta_of_nonpos`).

3929.doc:
The book's Fourier transform `f̂(t) = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} e(-xt) f(x) dx` ([H, §2.3], repeated in §7.1),
with `e(x) = e^{2πix}` (the repo's `TernaryGoldbach.e`).

393.doc:
**[H, Theorem 7.1.1]**, as printed (p. 138). It is stated only: neither this file nor the
repository proves it, and the repository does not use it.

How the statement is transcribed:
* "`x` a real number `≥ 10⁸`": `x : ℝ` with `10 ^ 8 ≤ x`.
* "`χ` a primitive Dirichlet character mod `q`, `1 ≤ q ≤ r`, where `r = 300000`": `q : ℕ` with
  `1 ≤ q` and `q ≤ 300000` (`r` is inlined), and `χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ q` with Mathlib's
  `χ.IsPrimitive` (conductor `= q`). This is the book's notion ([H, §2.2]): a character of
  `(ℤ/qℤ)*` lifted to `ℤ`, not induced from a smaller modulus. For `q = 1` it is the trivial
  character, which is primitive.
* "`δ ∈ ℝ` with `|δ| ≤ 4r/q`": `δ : ℝ` with `|δ| ≤ 4 * 300000 / q` in `ℝ`.
* The series `∑_{n=1}^∞` is the `tsum` over `n : ℕ+`, with the factors in the printed order
  `Λ(n) χ(n) e((δ/x) n) e^{-(n/x)²/2}`. `Λ` is Mathlib's von Mangoldt function and
  `χ(n) = χ(n mod q)`. The weight is written as printed, `e^{-(n/x)²/2}`; for `n ≥ 1` it equals
  `η♥(n/x)` under either reading of `η♥`. The terms are bounded by `log n · e^{-(n/x)²/2}`, so the
  series converges absolutely and the `tsum` is its sum.
* `I_{q=1}` is `if q = 1 then 1 else 0`.
* `η̂♥(-δ)` is `thm_7_1_1_hat thm_7_1_1_etaHeart (-δ)`: the book's Fourier normalization applied
  to the one-sided Gaussian, which is the book's convention (see `thm_7_1_1_remark`). It equals
  `∫₀^∞ e(δt) e^{-t²/2} dt` (`thm_7_1_1_hat_etaHeart`), the main term `G_δ(1)` of
  [H, Lemma 9.1.1]. It is *not* the remark's `√(2π) e^{-2π²δ²}` (`thm_7_1_1_remark_ne`). With that
  value the statement is false (`thm_7_1_1_main_remark_false`).
* `E` is a complex number, quantified after `x, q, χ, δ`, so it may depend on them. It satisfies
  the printed identity `sum = I_{q=1} · η̂♥(-δ) · x + E · x`, and `|E|` becomes `‖E‖ ≤
  4.306e-22 + 1 / √x * (650400 / √q + 112)`. The decimal literals are exact rationals.
* There is no hypothesis beyond the printed ones. Platt's GRH verification, which the book's
  proof uses (§9.6, `T₀ = 10⁸/q`), is not an assumption of the statement.

3930.doc:
**[H, Corollary 7.1.3], as printed.**

How the statement is transcribed:
* `η`, `η₂`, `η₁` are the book's objects `cor_7_1_3_eta`, `cor_7_1_3_eta2`, `cor_7_1_3_eta1`,
  built from the printed definitions. `η̂` is `cor_7_1_3_hat cor_7_1_3_eta`, with the book's
  normalization of the Fourier transform. Since `η` vanishes on `(-∞, 0]`, this is the Fourier
  transform of the weight on `ℝ⁺` extended by zero.
* "`x` a real number `≥ 10⁸`": `x : ℝ` with `10 ^ 8 ≤ x`.
* "`χ` a primitive character mod `q`, `1 ≤ q ≤ r`, where `r = 300000`": `q : ℕ` with `1 ≤ q` and
  `q ≤ 300000` (`r` is inlined), and `χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ q` with Mathlib's `χ.IsPrimitive`
  (conductor `= q`). This is the book's notion ([H, §2.2]): a character of `(ℤ/qℤ)*` lifted to `ℤ`,
  vanishing on `n` with `(n, q) ≠ 1`, and not induced by a character of smaller modulus. For `q = 1`
  it is the trivial character, which is primitive.
* "`δ ∈ ℝ` with `|δ| ≤ 4r/q`": `δ : ℝ` with `|δ| ≤ 4 * 300000 / q` in `ℝ`.
* The series `∑_{n=1}^∞` is the `tsum` over `n : ℕ+`, with the factors in the printed order
  `Λ(n) χ(n) e((δ/x) n) η(n/x)`. `Λ` is Mathlib's von Mangoldt function and `χ(n) = χ(n mod q)`.
  The series converges absolutely (`η` has Gaussian decay), so the `tsum` is its sum.
* `I_{q=1}` is `if q = 1 then 1 else 0`.
* `E` is a complex number, quantified after `x, q, χ, δ`, so it may depend on them. It satisfies
  the printed identity `sum = I_{q=1} · η̂(-δ) · x + E · x`, and its modulus `‖E‖` is at most
  `2.485e-19 + 1 / √x * (381500 / √q + 76)`. The decimal literals are exact rationals.
* No hypothesis beyond the printed ones. Platt's verification, which the book's proof uses, is not
  an assumption of the statement.

40.doc:
The `vonMangoldt` function is the function on natural numbers that returns `log p` if the input can
be expressed as `p^k` for a prime `p`.
In the case when `n` is a prime power, `Nat.minFac` will give the appropriate prime, as it is the
smallest prime factor.

In the `ArithmeticFunction` locale, we have the notation `Λ` for this function.
This is also available in the `ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt` locale, allowing for selective
access to the notation.

4065.doc:
The constant `c_E = γ + Σ_{p ≥ 2} (log p)/(p(p − 1))` of [H, (12.14)] (`eq:garno`), used in
[H, Cor. 12.2.5].  Defined by the series, as printed; the decimal value `1.3325822…` that [H]
quotes is not part of the definition.  The sum runs over the primes (`Nat.Primes`); it converges
(`cor_12_2_5_cE_summable`), so the `tsum` is the true sum.  `γ` is Mathlib's
`Real.eulerMascheroniConstant`.  It equals the repo's `TernaryGoldbach.Prelim.RamPf.cR`
(`cor_12_2_5_cE_eq_cR`), so the repo's bounds give `1.3325822 ≤ c_E ≤ 1.3325823`
(`cor_12_2_5_cE_bounds`).  This is *not* the repo's `TernaryGoldbach.MinorArcs.cE`, which is the
rounded-down rational `1.33258` (`cor_12_2_5_cE_round_down`).

4066.doc:
The hypotheses of [H, Cor. 12.2.5] on the coefficients: "`{aₙ}_{n=1}^∞`, `aₙ ∈ ℂ`, supported
on the primes; `{aₙ} ∈ ℓ₁ ∩ ℓ₂`; `aₙ = 0` for `n ≤ √x`", transcribed clause by clause (the `ℓ₂`
clause is redundant, as `ℓ₁ ⊆ ℓ₂`, but is kept as printed).  The sequence is `a : ℕ → ℂ`; the
extra index `0` is harmless, since `a 0 = 0` is forced both by prime support and by
`0 ≤ √x`.  Equivalent to the repo's `TernaryGoldbach.MinorArcs.PrimeSupported x a`
(`cor_12_2_5_coeffs_iff`).

4067.doc:
The arcs `𝔐` of [H, (12.1)] (`eq:jokor`, in Prop. 12.1.1), used in the first display of
[H, Cor. 12.2.5]:
`𝔐 = ⋃_{q ≤ Q₀} ⋃_{a mod q, (a,q)=1} (a/q − δ₀r/qx, a/q + δ₀r/qx)`.

*Reading.* The printed (12.1) has a radius `δ₀r/(qx)` with an `r` that Prop. 12.1.1 never
introduces (a leftover from (10.5), where `r` is the parameter of `𝔐_{δ₀,r}`; the 2013 preprint
has the same `r`).  We read `r = Q₀`: this is what the proof of Prop. 12.1.1 integrates over
((12.3): `|α| ≤ δ₀Q₀/qx`), and it makes `𝔐` the analogue of `𝔐_{δ₀,Q₀}` without the
odd/even distinction.

*Encoding.* Not in the repo (Prop. 12.1.1 is not formalized), so defined here, in exactly the
encoding of the repo's `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.majorArcs`: the arcs are lifted from `ℝ/ℤ` to
`ℝ` by letting `a` run over *all* integers coprime to `q` (so the set is 1-periodic and is the
preimage of [H]'s subset of `ℝ/ℤ`), `q` runs over `1 ≤ q ≤ Q₀`, `(a, q) = 1` is
`IsCoprime (a : ℤ) q`, and the arcs are open intervals.

4068.doc:
**[H, Corollary 12.2.5]**, as printed (both displays, the second being (12.42)).

Transcription choices:
* `x δ₀ Q₀ : ℝ` and `a : ℕ → ℂ` are universally quantified; the hypotheses on `{aₙ}` are
  `cor_12_2_5_coeffs x a` (see there).
* `Q₀ ≥ 10⁵`, `δ₀ ≥ 1` and `(20000 Q₀)² ≤ x/2δ₀` are verbatim, reading `x/2δ₀` as `x/(2δ₀)`
  (as in `Q = √(x/2δ₀)`).  Together they force `x > 0`, which [H] leaves implicit.
* "set `Q = √(x/2δ₀)`" is the local definition `let Q := √(x / (2 * δ₀))`.
* `S(α) = Σₙ aₙ e(αn)` is the repo's `TernaryGoldbach.expTsum a α = ∑' n, a n * e (n * α)`,
  with `TernaryGoldbach.e t = exp(2πit)`, which is [H]'s `e(t) = e^{2πit}`; the series
  converges absolutely because `a ∈ ℓ₁`.
* `∫_{𝔐} |S(α)|² dα`, for `𝔐 ⊆ ℝ/ℤ`, is the Lebesgue integral of `‖S α‖ ^ 2` over
  `(0,1] ∩ 𝔐̃`, where `𝔐̃ ⊆ ℝ` is the 1-periodic preimage of `𝔐`.  As `(0,1]` is a fundamental
  domain, this is the integral for the Haar probability measure on `ℝ/ℤ` (the measure for which
  [H] writes `∫_{ℝ/ℤ} |S|² = Σ |aₙ|²`).
* First display: `𝔐` is (12.1), `cor_12_2_5_arcs δ₀ Q₀ x` (with [H]'s undefined `r` read as
  `Q₀`, see there); the condition `Q₀ ≤ Q^{0.6}` uses the real power `Q ^ (0.6 : ℝ)`.
* Second display (12.42): `𝔐_{δ₀,Q₀}` is (10.5) with `r = Q₀`, i.e. the repo's
  `TernaryGoldbach.Helfgott.majorArcs δ₀ Q₀ x`, checked against the LaTeX of (10.5): radius
  `δ₀r/2qx` around `a/q` for odd `q ≤ r`, radius `δ₀r/qx` for even `q ≤ 2r`, `(a, q) = 1`, open
  intervals, lifted to `ℝ` as for (12.1).  The condition `(2Q₀) ≤ (2Q)^{0.6}` uses the real
  power; `log 2Q₀` and `log 2Q` are `log (2Q₀)` and `log (2Q)`.
* `c₊ = 1.36` is the literal `1.36`; `c_E` is `cor_12_2_5_cE`, defined by its series.
* `Σₙ |aₙ|²` is `∑' n, ‖a n‖ ^ 2` (a convergent series, as `a ∈ ℓ₂`).

4077.doc: `by tac` constructs a term of the expected type by running the tactic(s) `tac`.

4078.doc:
Introduces one or more hypotheses, optionally naming and/or pattern-matching them.
For each hypothesis to be introduced, the remaining main goal's target type must
be a `let` or function type.

* `intro` by itself introduces one anonymous hypothesis, which can be accessed
  by e.g. `assumption`. It is equivalent to `intro _`.
* `intro x y` introduces two hypotheses and names them. Individual hypotheses
  can be anonymized via `_`, given a type ascription, or matched against a pattern:
  ```lean
  -- ... ⊢ α × β → ...
  intro (a, b)
  -- ..., a : α, b : β ⊢ ...
  ```
* `intro rfl` is short for `intro h; subst h`, if `h` is an equality where the left-hand or right-hand side
  is a variable.
* Alternatively, `intro` can be combined with pattern matching much like `fun`:
  ```lean
  intro
  | n + 1, 0 => tac
  | ...
  ```

4081.doc:
`rcases` is a tactic that will perform `cases` recursively, according to a pattern. It is used to
destructure hypotheses or expressions composed of inductive types like `h1 : a ∧ b ∧ c ∨ d` or
`h2 : ∃ x y, trans_rel R x y`. Usual usage might be `rcases h1 with ⟨ha, hb, hc⟩ | hd` or
`rcases h2 with ⟨x, y, _ | ⟨z, hxz, hzy⟩⟩` for these examples.

Each element of an `rcases` pattern is matched against a particular local hypothesis (most of which
are generated during the execution of `rcases` and represent individual elements destructured from
the input expression). An `rcases` pattern has the following grammar:

* A name like `x`, which names the active hypothesis as `x`.
* A blank `_`, which does nothing (letting the automatic naming system used by `cases` name the
  hypothesis).
* A hyphen `-`, which clears the active hypothesis and any dependents.
* The keyword `rfl`, which expects the hypothesis to be `h : a = b`, and calls `subst` on the
  hypothesis (which has the effect of replacing `b` with `a` everywhere or vice versa).
* A type ascription `p : ty`, which sets the type of the hypothesis to `ty` and then matches it
  against `p`. (Of course, `ty` must unify with the actual type of `h` for this to work.)
* A tuple pattern `⟨p1, p2, p3⟩`, which matches a constructor with many arguments, or a series
  of nested conjunctions or existentials. For example if the active hypothesis is `a ∧ b ∧ c`,
  then the conjunction will be destructured, and `p1` will be matched against `a`, `p2` against `b`
  and so on.
* A `@` before a tuple pattern as in `@⟨p1, p2, p3⟩` will bind all arguments in the constructor,
  while leaving the `@` off will only use the patterns on the explicit arguments.
* An alternation pattern `p1 | p2 | p3`, which matches an inductive type with multiple constructors,
  or a nested disjunction like `a ∨ b ∨ c`.

A pattern like `⟨a, b, c⟩ | ⟨d, e⟩` will do a split over the inductive datatype,
naming the first three parameters of the first constructor as `a,b,c` and the
first two of the second constructor `d,e`. If the list is not as long as the
number of arguments to the constructor or the number of constructors, the
remaining variables will be automatically named. If there are nested brackets
such as `⟨⟨a⟩, b | c⟩ | d` then these will cause more case splits as necessary.
If there are too many arguments, such as `⟨a, b, c⟩` for splitting on
`∃ x, ∃ y, p x`, then it will be treated as `⟨a, ⟨b, c⟩⟩`, splitting the last
parameter as necessary.

`rcases` also has special support for quotient types: quotient induction into Prop works like
matching on the constructor `quot.mk`.

`rcases h : e with PAT` will do the same as `rcases e with PAT` with the exception that an
assumption `h : e = PAT` will be added to the context.

4086.doc:
The unique meromorphic function `ℂ → ℂ` which agrees with `∑' n : ℕ, χ n / n ^ s` wherever the
latter is convergent. This is constructed as a linear combination of Hurwitz zeta functions.

Note that this is not the same as `LSeries χ`: they agree in the convergence range, but
`LSeries χ s` is defined to be `0` if `re s ≤ 1`.

4094.doc:
The `have` tactic is for adding opaque definitions and hypotheses to the local context of the main goal.
The definitions forget their associated value and cannot be unfolded, unlike definitions added by the `let` tactic.

* `have h : t := e` adds the hypothesis `h : t` if `e` is a term of type `t`.
* `have h := e` uses the type of `e` for `t`.
* `have : t := e` and `have := e` use `this` for the name of the hypothesis.
* `have pat := e` for a pattern `pat` is equivalent to `match e with | pat => _`,
  where `_` stands for the tactics that follow this one.
  It is convenient for types that have only one applicable constructor.
  For example, given `h : p ∧ q ∧ r`, `have ⟨h₁, h₂, h₃⟩ := h` produces the
  hypotheses `h₁ : p`, `h₂ : q`, and `h₃ : r`.
* The syntax `have (eq := h) pat := e` is equivalent to `match h : e with | pat => _`,
  which adds the equation `h : e = pat` to the local context.

The tactic supports all the same syntax variants and options as the `have` term.

## Properties and relations

* It is not possible to unfold a variable introduced using `have`, since the definition's value is forgotten.
  The `let` tactic introduces definitions that can be unfolded.
* The `have h : t := e` is like doing `let h : t := e; clear_value h`.
* The `have` tactic is preferred for propositions, and `let` is preferred for non-propositions.
* Sometimes `have` is used for non-propositions to ensure that the variable is never unfolded,
  which may be important for performance reasons.
    Consider using the equivalent `let +nondep` to indicate the intent.

4095.doc:
Assuming `x` is a variable in the local context with an inductive type,
`induction x` applies induction on `x` to the main goal,
producing one goal for each constructor of the inductive type,
in which the target is replaced by a general instance of that constructor
and an inductive hypothesis is added for each recursive argument to the constructor.
If the type of an element in the local context depends on `x`,
that element is reverted and reintroduced afterward,
so that the inductive hypothesis incorporates that hypothesis as well.

For example, given `n : Nat` and a goal with a hypothesis `h : P n` and target `Q n`,
`induction n` produces one goal with hypothesis `h : P 0` and target `Q 0`,
and one goal with hypotheses `h : P (Nat.succ a)` and `ih₁ : P a → Q a` and target `Q (Nat.succ a)`.
Here the names `a` and `ih₁` are chosen automatically and are not accessible.
You can use `with` to provide the variables names for each constructor.
- `induction e`, where `e` is an expression instead of a variable,
  generalizes `e` in the goal, and then performs induction on the resulting variable.
- `induction e using r` allows the user to specify the principle of induction that should be used.
  Here `r` should be a term whose result type must be of the form `C t`,
  where `C` is a bound variable and `t` is a (possibly empty) sequence of bound variables
- `induction e generalizing z₁ ... zₙ`, where `z₁ ... zₙ` are variables in the local context,
  generalizes over `z₁ ... zₙ` before applying the induction but then introduces them in each goal.
  In other words, the net effect is that each inductive hypothesis is generalized.
- Given `x : Nat`, `induction x with | zero => tac₁ | succ x' ih => tac₂`
  uses tactic `tac₁` for the `zero` case, and `tac₂` for the `succ` case.

4096.doc:
After `with`, there is an optional tactic that runs on all branches, and
then a list of alternatives.

4097.doc:
Zero, the smallest natural number.

Using `Nat.zero` explicitly should usually be avoided in favor of the literal `0`, which is the
[simp normal form](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=simp-normal-forms).

4098.doc:
The `simp` tactic uses lemmas and hypotheses to simplify the main goal target or
non-dependent hypotheses. It has many variants:
- `simp` simplifies the main goal target using lemmas tagged with the attribute `[simp]`.
- `simp [h₁, h₂, ..., hₙ]` simplifies the main goal target using the lemmas tagged
  with the attribute `[simp]` and the given `hᵢ`'s, where the `hᵢ`'s are expressions.-
- If an `hᵢ` is a defined constant `f`, then `f` is unfolded. If `f` has equational lemmas associated
  with it (and is not a projection or a `reducible` definition), these are used to rewrite with `f`.
- `simp [*]` simplifies the main goal target using the lemmas tagged with the
  attribute `[simp]` and all hypotheses.
- `simp only [h₁, h₂, ..., hₙ]` is like `simp [h₁, h₂, ..., hₙ]` but does not use `[simp]` lemmas.
- `simp [-id₁, ..., -idₙ]` simplifies the main goal target using the lemmas tagged
  with the attribute `[simp]`, but removes the ones named `idᵢ`.
- `simp at h₁ h₂ ... hₙ` simplifies the hypotheses `h₁ : T₁` ... `hₙ : Tₙ`. If
  the target or another hypothesis depends on `hᵢ`, a new simplified hypothesis
  `hᵢ` is introduced, but the old one remains in the local context.
- `simp at *` simplifies all the hypotheses and the target.
- `simp [*] at *` simplifies target and all (propositional) hypotheses using the
  other hypotheses.

4099.doc:
The `omega` tactic, for resolving integer and natural linear arithmetic problems.

It is not yet a full decision procedure (no "dark" or "grey" shadows),
but should be effective on many problems.

We handle hypotheses of the form `x = y`, `x < y`, `x ≤ y`, and `k ∣ x` for `x y` in `Nat` or `Int`
(and `k` a literal), along with negations of these statements.

We decompose the sides of the inequalities as linear combinations of atoms.

If we encounter `x / k` or `x % k` for literal integers `k` we introduce new auxiliary variables
and the relevant inequalities.

On the first pass, we do not perform case splits on natural subtraction.
If `omega` fails, we recursively perform a case split on
a natural subtraction appearing in a hypothesis, and try again.

The options
```
omega +splitDisjunctions +splitNatSub +splitNatAbs +splitMinMax
```
can be used to:
* `splitDisjunctions`: split any disjunctions found in the context,
  if the problem is not otherwise solvable.
* `splitNatSub`: for each appearance of `((a - b : Nat) : Int)`, split on `a ≤ b` if necessary.
* `splitNatAbs`: for each appearance of `Int.natAbs a`, split on `0 ≤ a` if necessary.
* `splitMinMax`: for each occurrence of `min a b`, split on `min a b = a ∨ min a b = b`

Currently, all of these are on by default.

41.doc:
`if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.


Conventions for notations in identifiers:

 * The recommended spelling of `if c then t else e` in identifiers is `ite` (use `left` for `t` and `right` for `e`).

This is the same as `byTactic`, but it uses a different syntax kind. This is
used by `show` and `suffices` instead of `byTactic` because these syntaxes don't
support arbitrary terms where `byTactic` is accepted. Mathport uses this to e.g.
safely find-replace `by exact $e` by `$e` in any context without causing
incorrect syntax when the full expression is `show $T by exact $e`.

4104.doc:
`ring` solves equations in *commutative* (semi)rings, allowing for variables in the
exponent. If the goal is not appropriate for `ring` (e.g. not an equality) `ring_nf` will be
suggested. See also `ring1`, which fails if the goal is not an equality.

* `ring!` will use a more aggressive reducibility setting to determine equality of atoms.

Examples:
```
example (n : ℕ) (m : ℤ) : 2^(n+1) * m = 2 * 2^n * m := by ring
example (a b : ℤ) (n : ℕ) : (a + b)^(n + 2) = (a^2 + b^2 + a * b + b * a) * (a + b)^n := by ring
example (x y : ℕ) : x + id y = y + id x := by ring!
example (x : ℕ) (h : x * 2 > 5): x + x > 5 := by ring; assumption -- suggests ring_nf
```

4110.doc:
`by_contra h` proves `⊢ p` by contradiction,
introducing a hypothesis `h : ¬p` and proving `False`.
* If `p` is a negation `¬q`, `h : q` will be introduced instead of `¬¬q`.
* If `p` is decidable, it uses `Decidable.byContradiction` instead of `Classical.byContradiction`.
* If `h` is omitted, the introduced variable will be called `this`.
* `h` can be any pattern supported by `rcases`/`rintro`.

4112.doc:
`Not p`, or `¬p`, is the negation of `p`. It is defined to be `p → False`,
so if your goal is `¬p` you can use `intro h` to turn the goal into
`h : p ⊢ False`, and if you have `hn : ¬p` and `h : p` then `hn h : False`
and `(hn h).elim` will prove anything.
For more information: [Propositional Logic](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/propositions_and_proofs.html#propositional-logic)


Conventions for notations in identifiers:

 * The recommended spelling of `¬` in identifiers is `not`.

4114.doc:
`subst x...` substitutes each hypothesis `x` with a definition found in the local context,
then eliminates the hypothesis.
- If `x` is a local definition, then its definition is used.
- Otherwise, if there is a hypothesis of the form `x = e` or `e = x`,
  then `e` is used for the definition of `x`.

If `h : a = b`, then `subst h` may be used if either `a` or `b` unfolds to a local hypothesis.
This is similar to the `cases h` tactic.

See also: `subst_vars` for substituting all local hypotheses that have a defining equation.

4126.doc:
Step-wise reasoning over transitive relations.
```
calc
  a = b := pab
  b = c := pbc
  ...
  y = z := pyz
```
proves `a = z` from the given step-wise proofs. `=` can be replaced with any
relation implementing the typeclass `Trans`. Instead of repeating the right-
hand sides, subsequent left-hand sides can be replaced with `_`.
```
calc
  a = b := pab
  _ = c := pbc
  ...
  _ = z := pyz
```
It is also possible to write the *first* relation as `<lhs>\n  _ = <rhs> :=
<proof>`. This is useful for aligning relation symbols, especially on longer
identifiers:
```
calc abc
  _ = bce := pabce
  _ = cef := pbcef
  ...
  _ = xyz := pwxyz
```

`calc` works as a term, as a tactic or as a `conv` tactic.

See [Theorem Proving in Lean 4][tpil4] for more information.

[tpil4]: https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#calculational-proofs

4132.doc:
`push_cast` rewrites the goal to move certain coercions (*casts*) inward, toward the leaf nodes.
This uses `norm_cast` lemmas in the forward direction.
For example, `↑(a + b)` will be written to `↑a + ↑b`.
- `push_cast` moves casts inward in the goal.
- `push_cast at h` moves casts inward in the hypothesis `h`.
It can be used with extra simp lemmas with, for example, `push_cast [Int.add_zero]`.

Example:
```lean
example (a b : Nat)
    (h1 : ((a + b : Nat) : Int) = 10)
    (h2 : ((a + b + 0 : Nat) : Int) = 10) :
    ((a + b : Nat) : Int) = 10 := by
  /-
  h1 : ↑(a + b) = 10
  h2 : ↑(a + b + 0) = 10
  ⊢ ↑(a + b) = 10
  -/
  push_cast
  /- Now
  ⊢ ↑a + ↑b = 10
  -/
  push_cast at h1
  push_cast [Int.add_zero] at h2
  /- Now
  h1 h2 : ↑a + ↑b = 10
  -/
  exact h1
```

See also `norm_cast`.

4133.doc:
`refine e` behaves like `exact e`, except that named (`?x`) or unnamed (`?_`)
holes in `e` that are not solved by unification with the main goal's target type
are converted into new goals, using the hole's name, if any, as the goal case name.

4135.doc:
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
